synth01.title: TemplateTransfer: ligand binding-site prediction by single-template pocket transplantation
synth01.text:
TemplateTransfer: ligand binding-site prediction by single-template pocket transplantation
TemplateTransfer predicts ligand binding sites by transplanting pockets from the single highest-identity template structure. On an invented benchmark of 80 targets it reaches 0.55 top-1 pocket precision when template identity exceeds 40%, but precision drops to 0.41 for targets below 30% identity, because a single template often carries a partially mismatched pocket.

synth02.title: SeqPocket: sequence-only binding-site prediction with a residue-attention network
synth02.text:
SeqPocket: sequence-only binding-site prediction with a residue-attention network
SeqPocket predicts binding residues directly from sequence using a residue-attention network, requiring no structural template. It matches template-based methods on targets with no usable template but lags them by 0.10 top-1 precision on template-rich targets. The authors note it cannot localize pockets that lack sequence motifs.

synth03.title: MultiTempl: naive pocket pooling from multiple templates
synth03.text:
MultiTempl: naive pocket pooling from multiple templates
MultiTempl pools predicted pockets from up to 8 template structures and ranks them by pocket frequency. Pooling raises recall by 0.15 over single-template transfer, but precision on low-identity targets stays flat because low-quality templates vote with equal weight.

synth04.title: GeoScore: geometry-based ranking of candidate binding pockets
synth04.text:
GeoScore: geometry-based ranking of candidate binding pockets
GeoScore ranks candidate pockets by geometric descriptors (depth, enclosure, hydrophobic patch area) without any template. It is fast and template-free, but the abstract reports no comparison against template-based predictors and no low-identity evaluation.

synth05.title: ConsenSite: consensus scoring of pockets across homologous structures
synth05.text:
ConsenSite: consensus scoring of pockets across homologous structures
ConsenSite scores candidate pockets by unweighted consensus across homologous experimental structures of the same protein. It improves precision by 0.07 over single-structure scoring, but requires multiple experimental structures of the target itself, which are unavailable for most prediction targets; it was not evaluated on template-based transfer.

synth06.title: A survey of binding-site prediction methods
synth06.text:
A survey of binding-site prediction methods
This survey groups binding-site predictors into template-based, geometry-based and sequence-based families, and observes that low-identity template transfer remains the weakest setting across all template-based methods surveyed.

facts.text: Title: PermaLig: consensus scoring across multiple template structures improves protein-ligand binding-site prediction on low-identity targets.
Problem: predicting ligand binding sites on proteins whose best available template shares less than 30% sequence identity with the target.
Setting: benchmark of 60 invented target proteins (SynBench-60), split into an easy subset (template identity >= 30%) and a hard subset (< 30%).

Method summary: PermaLig collects the top 5 template structures per target, transfers putative pockets from each, and scores each candidate pocket by a consensus vote weighted by per-template local quality (measured by an invented local quality score, LQS).
Contribution 1: a multi-template consensus scoring scheme in which each candidate pocket is voted on by up to 5 templates weighted by LQS (Fig 1 shows the pipeline).
Contribution 2: on the hard subset of SynBench-60, PermaLig reaches 0.61 top-1 pocket precision versus 0.48 for the best single-template baseline (Fig 2, invented numbers for demo).
Contribution 3: an ablation showing that consensus scoring contributes +0.09 top-1 precision over simple template ranking on the hard subset (Fig 2).
Limitations stated by the authors: evaluation is limited to single-chain soluble proteins; no membrane proteins were tested; LQS weights were tuned on the same benchmark.
Data availability: SynBench-60 targets, predictions and scripts are stated to be available in an invented repository.
Fig 1: pipeline diagram of PermaLig (template selection, pocket transfer, LQS-weighted consensus voting).
Fig 2: benchmark results and ablation bar chart on SynBench-60 easy/hard subsets.
No claim of superiority on membrane proteins.
No claim that LQS is better than other quality scores; no comparison with other quality scores was run.
